primary_metric: exact-match pass_rate vs the rubric truth (uniform rubric, see spec.json)
headline: The skill lifts ALL THREE tiers to 1.000 (24/24). Baseline rises with model size (Haiku 0.667 < Sonnet 0.792 < Opus 0.875), so the lift is largest where the model is weakest: Haiku +0.333, Sonnet +0.208, Opus +0.125. With the skill, Haiku 4.5 matches Opus 4.8.

cost.note: with_skill adds ~7-8k tokens (the two file reads, ~2 tool calls) at every tier. Haiku+skill is the cheapest AND fastest path to 8/8 — ~33.6k tokens / ~15s — well under Opus baseline's 33.2k tokens at a worse score.

per_item_baseline._legend: correct_count / 3 per model, baseline condition (with_skill is 3/3 on every item at every tier)

1.note: Haiku/Sonnet each had one run prescribe a Convex .filter pushdown (the misconception); Opus never did

2.note: Date.now()-in-query — Haiku mostly missed it (blamed reactivity/'not cached'); clear size gradient

3.note: runAction same-runtime overhead — Haiku struggled to name the runtime-crossing rule / plain-helper fix

4.note: control — transaction isolation well-known at every tier

7.note: UNIVERSAL discriminator — every baseline run at every tier justified 'it's fine' via index-narrowing, never the .paginate() exception. with_skill 3/3 everywhere.

findings: Item 7 (the .paginate() .filter exception) is a hard discriminator at EVERY model size: 0/9 baseline runs got it, 9/9 with_skill runs did. No tier knows this rule from priors; the skill supplies it.
The smaller the model, the more the skill helps: it back-fills items (2,3 for Haiku; 1,2 for Sonnet) that the larger model already knew, on top of the universal item-7 lift.

With the skill, tier no longer matters for this task — Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus all reach 24/24. This is the 'steer a cheap model to a strong-model result' pattern: Haiku+skill (~33.6k tok, ~15s) beats Opus baseline (0.875) on both score and cost.
